evals.name: Identifies structured logging and correlation ID requirements
evals.prompt: I'm building a new checkout API endpoint that processes payments. It calls Stripe, updates our database, and sends a confirmation email. What logging should I add to make sure I can debug production issues?
evals.expected_output: The model should recommend structured JSON logging with stable event names, correlation/request IDs propagated across all operations, and warn against logging secrets or full request bodies.
assertions: The output recommends structured logging (JSON objects with event names) rather than string interpolation.
The output explicitly requires correlation IDs or request IDs to be generated and propagated across all log lines and outbound calls.
The output warns against logging secrets, tokens, passwords, or full PII/payment data.
The output defines appropriate log levels (error, warn, info, debug) for different event types.

assertions.prompt: Does the output demonstrate awareness of structured logging, correlation IDs, RED metrics, or alerting best practices — not just generic 'add logging' advice? It should reference specific steps or concepts from the observability-and-instrumentation workflow.

evals._mutation_check: Break by: removing the structured logging assertion (assertion 1) and replacing with 'output mentions logging'. Expected: eval should fail with score < 0.5 because the agent could pass by suggesting console.log statements without structured logging.

evals.name: Recognizes metric cardinality pitfalls and recommends RED metrics
evals.prompt: My team wants to track request latency for our REST API. Someone suggested using user_id as a label on our Prometheus metrics so we can debug per-user issues. Is this a good idea?
evals.expected_output: The model should strongly advise against using user_id as a metric label due to cardinality explosion, explain why unbounded label values crash metrics backends, and recommend RED metrics with bounded labels instead.
assertions: The output identifies user_id as a metric label as a cardinality bomb that will crash the metrics backend.
The output recommends bounded labels (route template, status class, method) instead of unbounded values.
The output recommends RED metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration) for endpoint instrumentation.
The output recommends histograms with percentiles (p50/p95/p99) instead of averages for latency.
The output clarifies that per-user debugging belongs in logs and traces, not metrics.
evals._mutation_check: Break by: removing the cardinality assertion (assertion 1) and replacing with 'output mentions metrics'. Expected: eval should fail with score < 0.5 because the agent could pass by discussing metrics without identifying the cardinality problem.

evals.name: Distinguishes symptom-based vs cause-based alerting
evals.prompt: Our DevOps team set up alerts for CPU > 80%, memory > 75%, and disk usage > 70%. But we keep getting paged at 3am and it turns out nothing is actually wrong. How should we fix our alerting?
evals.expected_output: The model should identify these as cause-based alerts that create noise, and recommend shifting to symptom-based alerts (error rate, latency, queue depth) that fire when users are actually impacted.
assertions: The output identifies CPU/memory/disk alerts as cause-based alerts that create noise.
The output recommends symptom-based alerts (error rate, p99 latency, queue age) instead.
The output states that every alert must be actionable with a runbook link.
The output recommends limiting alert severities to two tiers (page and ticket).
The output explains that cause-based alerts fire when nothing is wrong and miss real user-facing failures.
